speechtext:
I should like to be permitted to lay on the table of the House certain information by way of reply to a question asked by the hon. member for Victoria (Mr. Tolmie) with respect to Japanese immigration. I promised him that it would be brought down to-day.
(The questions and answers are as follows) :
Questions:
1.	Under what conditions and regulations are Japanese immigrants admitted into Canada?
2.	In what way are the rights of Canadians in Japan limited as to ownership of land, franchise, mercantile ' pursuits, fishing, shipping (coastwise and foreign), mining, agriculture, and other pursuits such as are engaged in by Japanese in Canada?
3.	What is the number of Japanese immigrants that have entered Canada yearly in each of the ten years ending March 31, 1922?
4.	How many Japanese have left Canada for Japan each year, during the same period?
5.	How many Japanese have returned to Canada from Japan each year during the same period?
Answers.
1.	Under a confidential Agreement known as the L/emieux Agreement entered into between Canada and Japan in the beginning of 1908. Under this Agreement Japan voluntarily restricts the movement of Japanese to Canada to a comparatively small number each year.
2.	In common with other foreigners, Canadians cannot as individuals own land in Japan. They can, however, if they form an association and become "juridical persons" under Japanese law. They further enjoy the rights of perpetual lease in respect of land in certain portions of the former foreign settlements in the open ports; and they may become holders of rights of "superficies" and "emphyteusis".
Foreigners have no franchise rights either in connection with elections to the Diet or to the prefectural, municipal, town, village or district assemblies.
Canadian vessels may not engage in the coasting trade between Japanese ports and Canadians may not become owners of ships flying the Japanese flag, though they may become members of "goshi-kwaisha" (partnership with limited and unlimited liability), "kabushiki-Kwaisha" (joint-stock companies), and "kabushiki-goshi-Kwaisha" (joint-stock partnerships with limited and unlimited liability) owning Japanese ships.
Canadians may not as individuals engage in mining, but a company formed under Japanese
law by foreigners and registered as a juridical person may do so.
They may not become shareholders of the Bank of Japan, the Yokohama Specie Bank, the Bank of Korea, the South Manchuria Railway Company, the Oriental Development Company and certain other companies, or of shipping Companies in receipt of a Government subsidy. They may not become members or brokers of the various exchanges in Japan. They may not as individuals become members of Japanese Chambers of Commerce. They may not engage in the emigration business or hold shares in any company so engaged.
Foreign unskilled labourers may not pursue their callings in Japan outside the limits of the former foreign settlements or the "mixed residence" areas without the express permission of the administrative authorities. Labourers for this purpose are defined as being persons engaged in labouring pursuits in connection with farming, fishing, mining, public works, building, manufacturing, transport, hauling (of vehicles), stevedoring and other forms of manual labour, but not persons in domestic service or persons following the calling of cooks and waiters.

Mr. T. L. CHURCH (North Toronto) moved for leave to introduce Bill No. 71 to amend the Railway Act, 1919.
Explain.

The object of the amendment is to restore the special rate that applied prior to the war in regard to tickets purchased on such special occasions as Thanksgiving Day and certain other holidays, and for the purpose of attendance at the fall fairs conventions and sporting events as are held throughout Canada. Before the war, single fares and h fare and a third was charged, instead of the full return fare, to persons attending various functions of this character on certain days and special occasions and conventions of different kinds held in the spring of the year by farmers' and other organizations. In connection with sporting events, such as soccer, lacrosse, football and hockey and other games, there was also a cut rate for week-ends. Now, I admit that during the war it was necessary, in the interest of economy, to curtail these concessions. But now that the war is over the people expect that after the country has spent some $900,000,000 directly and indirectly in aid of the railways of the country they shall be given some privileges in return besides the privilege of being always called upon to pay taxes. The United States have

restored the old special rates that obtained for these events prior to the war with the result that there has been a large increase in the earnings of the railways from this class of traffic.
I might read two or three sentences from certain letters I have received in reference to this matter. Mr. J. Lockie Wilson, the Superintendent of the Ontario Department of Agriculture, who has the supervision of some 360 fairs in the province of Ontario, urges the restoration of the old rate in the interests of these fairs which have a distinct educational value and make for the general good of the country. Mr. John G. Kent, the Managing Director of the Canadian National Exhibition Association, writes:
The public are clamouring for a return to pre-war eomdlitions, amd we have been urged by letter and personal interview from all parts of the country to bring before the Government the necessity of reducing regular fares for these various occasions.
Mr. P. J. Mulqueen, president of the Royal Canadian Henley and chairman of the Ontario Athletic Commission, also writes urging a restoration of the old special rates to prevent unrest and encourage sport and recreation. And Mr. A. P. Westervelt, Secretary of the Royal Agricultural Winter Fair, urges that steps be taken to restore the old rates. There is

he says-a general and insistent demand in this matter, and I would move that the bill be given its first reading.
Motion agreed to and bill read the first time.

Mr. GEORGE W. KYTE (Cape Breton South and Richmond) : I desire to add a word of explanation to what the hon. member for Brome has said. As soon as my attention was called to the fact that he

had voted in violation of the understood pair which he held, I had the pair with the hon. member for West Hastings transferred to the hon. member for South Perth (Mr. Forrester), and he did not vote.

These two gentlemen were paired also. The junior member for Halifax voted on the amendment, and as soon as my attention was called to it I communicated with him, so he did not vote on the main motion. The same thing happened with the hon. member for Drummond and Arthabaska. The junior member for Halifax has not been in the House for some weeks owing to the unfortunate condition of his health. He entered the Chamber at the last moment yesterday evening and I had no opportunity to remind him of his pair. I was unable to substitute another pair in his place because at that time the vote was proceeding along the furthest end of the rear row.
I did not observe these hon. members were voting in violation of their pairs because my attention was absorbed in the business of checking off the vote as it was called; otherwise I would have prevented the unfortunate incident. But by way of extenuation I need only cite the fact that the hon. member for West York (Sir Henry Drayton) also inadvertently voted. It is evident therefore that these errors may be committed even with the best intentions.
I do not know whether it is in order for me to add a word or two, Mr. Speaker.

On the motion of Hon Ernest Lapointe (Minister of Marine and Fisheries) the House went into committee to consider the following proposed resolutions, Mr. Gordon in the Chair:
1.	Resolved, That It is expedient to provide that the Governor in Council may, from time to time, advance and pay to the Corporation of Quebec Harbour Commissioners, hereinafter called the Corporation, such sums of money, not exceeding in the whole the sum of one million five hundred thousand dollars, as are required to enable the Corporation to carry on the construction of such terminal facilities as are necessary to properly equip the Port of Quebec.
2.	Resolved, That during the period of construction of the terminal facilities mentioned in these Resolutions, the interest payable on the debentures receivable by the Minister of Finance in exchange for such advances, shall be deemed to be money required to construct and to be part of the cost of construction of the said terminal facilites, and such interest may be paid out of the said sum of one million five hundred thousand dollars.
3.	Resolved, That the Corporation shall submit to the Minister of Marine and Fisheries for approval, monthly applications for such advances, with statements showing total expenditure on different items in detail, and upon approval, authority for the payment of the amount applied for may be granted by the Governor in Council.
4.	Resolved, That the Corporation shall, upon any advances being made, deposit with the Minister of Finance debentures of the Corporation equal in par value to the advance so made, repayable within twenty-four years from the date of issue, and bearing interest payable halfyearly at the rate of five per centum per annum.
5.	Resolved, That the principal and interest of any sums advanced under any Act founded on these resolutions, shall be payable by the Corporation out of all its property, assets, tools, rates, dues, penalties and other sources of revenue and income whatsoever, and shall be a charge thereon next after, and have precedence in regard to payment next after, ail debentures or bonds issued by the Corporation amounting to the sum of one million one hundred and fifty thousand dollars, under Chapter forty-eight of the Statutes of 1898, Chapter thirty-four of the Statutes of 1899, and Chapter thirty-six of the Statutes of 1907.

I would like to ask the minister if in his judgment the present volume of business done at the port of Quebec would indicate that the corporation would be able to meet the interest charges on a capitalization of this amount?

I do not expect that the Harbour Commissioners of Quebec will

Quebec Harbour
be able to meet the interest charges in the near future, but judging by the increase in the revenue during the last few year^, I think we may expect that they will be able to do so in a few years from now. In 1913, when advances were made by the former government to the present Harbour Commission the receipts were $226,000. The receipts have increased gradually up till last year, when they amounted to $387,323.91, almost one hundred per cent increase over 1913. The port of Quebec is the head of navigation for the big transatlantic liners, and as my hon. friend knows, the tendency of the shipping companies nowadays is to increase rather than reduce the size of their vessels. There is another consideration which we must not lose sight of, and it is that perhaps the finest portion of the harbour of Quebec is consecrated to the immigration purposes of the Canadian Government, for which the port receives not one cent from the Canadian Government. This comprises 800 feet of the finest part of the harbour, and the commissioners have to expend money to make the necessary repairs and to provide all the facilities required for immigration purposes. Of course, there is a bill standing in the books of the commission against the federal government on that account. This bill has never been paid, and I do not expect that it ever will be. It is quite clear that the expenditure to keep the harbour of Quebec in good condition must be met by the Government. The port of Quebec is in a position by itself, with the exception of Montreal and Vancouver, where improvements are made under the same conditions. In Toronto, the Government does not make advances to the Harbour Commission, but all the work is done by the Public Works Department. The money is not loaned and we do not expect any interest or anything of that kind. In Halifax, the harbour improvements are made by the Railways and Canals Department, and in St. John by the Public Works Department. On account of conditions at the port of Quebec, the port was administered by a corporation prior to Confederation, which was called the Trinity House. In 1875 the powers and the property of the Trinity House were transferred to a commission called the Quebec Harbour Commission, composed of nine members. Different public bodies were represented on that commission, which worked up until 1912, when the government of the day, wisely, I think, reduced 93
the commission to three, the number in Montreal, and since that time Quebec harbour has been under the control and administration of a harbour commission composed of three members. If the same plan were followed with Quebec harbour as with other ports, there would simply be an appropriation in the estimates of the Public Works Department, and we would hear no more about it, but so far as Quebec is concerned we have to make advances to the commission, bearing interest, which will be paid back if the port pays its way in the future.
In Montreal, I am pleased to say, the harbour is paying its own way. There is a resolution on the Order Paper for an advance of $5,000,000 to the port of Montreal. In the case of both these ports the resolution does not mean that the amount specified will be expended in one or two or three or four years. It simply enables the Government to make advances as required, and every item of improvement has to be approved by the Governor in Council before the advance is made. As I said, Montreal harbour is paying its own way and earning sufficient revenue to meet all the interest charges. They have already entered into contracts with the shipping companies providing for the payment of interest on the advances which are going to be made under the resolution standing on the Order Paper. I hope that in a few years Quebec harbour will be in just as prosperous a condition as Montreal.
Is it the intention of the Government to protect the workers who will be employed by the Quebec Harbour Commission, by insisting on a fair wage clause in all contracts entered into by the Commission?

I am myself agreeable to having a fair wage clause in all government contracts, but I do not know that it would be wise to provide for that in this resolution. That will be a matter between the Government and the Harbour Commissioners.

I put the question because heretofore in connection with money expended on the Ballan-tyne pier in Vancouver, and I believe in Montreal also, there has been trouble owing to the lack of such a clause in the contract.

I have a great deal of sympathy with the very natural aspirations of the port of Quebec. They

Quebec Harbour

have a magnificent harbour, and splendid facilities. The trouble is they cannot get people to use them, not that they lack the harbour, the water, or the facilities. There is a great grain elevator in Quebec with a capacity of two million bushels-with an outward loading capacity of sixty thousand bushels per hour, and with an unloading capacity for vessels-and the loading capacity from the cars is probably greater~of thirty thousand bushels an hour. As I say, they have a good equipment there. The matter has come before me in more than one way; it has come before me in the past as chairman of the Railway Board when questions as to rates, facilities, and similar matters have been up for consideration, and I have also had to do with it as Minister of Finance. The great difficulty with Quebec has been this: Take for example the grain trade in particular. The shippers of grain like to hold their grain at points where they can get just as many markets as possible, and efforts have been made from time to time to induce the grain trade to make some right use of this first great facility that is open to them; but I confess that the efforts made-and I was a party to them-have been unsuccessful. Now if I thought that another million and a half would do any good to that grain business; if I thought another million and a half would be of any real use to the Quebec harbour, and to the commerce of this country, and would be effective in inducing people to ship there who do not now do so, why the matter would be open for further consideration. But, as I see it, that port is pretty well equipped to-day. Furthermore the port has been well looked after so far as capital expenditure is concerned. The country has advanced it over $11,000,000. There is to-day more than $11,000,000 owing, moneys advanced to the Quebec Harbour Commission, As the account has been running for some time there are arrears of interest due which now amount to $6,251,000, so that we have been going behind very steadily and very regularly in connection with this particular investment. It is perfectly true that part of these facilities are of use in other directions rather than directly in relation to government activities. My hon. friend (Mr. Lapointe) is perfectly right when he says that first rate facilities are given there for immigrants. There is no doubt about that and there is no doubt also that part of the harbour he mentions, eight hundred feet is being used. Neither is there any doubt about the contra accounts. There are

contra accounts, but they fall very far short of giving us any satisfactory reason why further investments in this direction should be made at the present moment. The Department of Public Works rent this immigration building, and there are arrears of rent in connection with it, from the year 1913 to the year 1921, amounting altogether to $455,209.04.
Is that a cross account?

Yes, a cross account. In the same way the Department of the Interior occupies ground belonging to the commissioners. Their arrears run back to the year 1892 and amount to $351,000. Besides that there are other small charges bringing up the total contra account to $813,365.23 as against the $6,251,000 of interest as to which the commissioners are in arrear to the Government.
My point, in the first instance, is that we ought to be very clear that we do some good by spending this money; and in the second instance that we should not spend it unless there is a real emergency requiring such expenditure at the present time, because this is not the happiest moment for incurring that large expenditure. In order to give the committee some idea of the small extent to which these large facilities are used, I would like to point out that the five grain berths of Quebec, which hon. gentlemen familiar with the port will know of, were used during the whole of last season-and last season as the minister tells us was improving; they were doing a little more business-for only four weeks out of the entire season. The trouble is not due to lack of facilities but lack of business; and if we are really to help the port of Quebec our efforts should be to see to it that business in some way or other is handled in such channels of trade and so made available as to give the port some use for the existing facilities. The mere installation of more facilities and adding to the amount of idle space is not going to help the harbour commissioners of Quebec but will only add to the tremendous load of overdue interest to which they are now subject.
I may say that the matter has stood for so long that two years ago (when I went over the capital assets of the country, with a view to trying to get out something like a fair and honest balance sheet, I was forced to remove from the books of the country these Quebec debentures. They were non-interest producing

Quebec Harbour
debentures; the investment was an absolute uncollectable, non-revenue producing debt. They were taken off the active assets of the country and at the present time are in suspense. Further I do not know exactly why the resolution is worded in the way in which it is. I think that is probably due to an oversight.
The hon. gentleman has mentioned a statement as to capital assets that he had prepared. Did he present that to the House, or has it been published?

Oh, yes, that statement is to be found in the Public Accounts for the year 1920, and also in the same blue book for the year 1921. As I recollect it the statement was also mentioned in the budget speech in the session of 1919-20.
A complete statement?

Yes, a complete statement; the whole thing was given. I do not exactly see why the resolution is drawn in the way it is. I mean that part of it where it says that the new bonds and debentures are to be a first charge upon the property and assets of the commission except, I think it is, $1,150,000. The fact is that so far as this country is concerned we now have advances running up to $11,000,000, and I do not know exactly why they should be made secondary to a subsequent advance. In all sincerity I submit to my hon. friend that this is not helping Quebec. It is merely providing for the expenditure of money for additional facilities where those already existing are not being used to-day; and I submit also that the country cannot afford a further experiment of this nature.

I do not wish to discuss this matter from a provincial but rather from a national standpoint. In my opinion the minister should give the committee further details as to this item. It is proposed to grant a million and a half dollars for terminal facilities for the harbour of Quebec. In addition, there is another resolution on the order1 paper calling for an advance of $5,000,000 for facilities for the harbour of Montreal. Regarding the first-named port I think the constitution of the harbour commission is all wrong; it has not been the success which it should have been. There should be a new charter, a non-political commission and co-ordination of control. They are not getting the results from the expenditure at Quebec that they should.
93i
The development of one harbour by the improvement of terminals should benefit all harbours, because they are all a link in a chain of communication of waterborne traffic. I had a return of the amount of money spent in various harbours in Canada, and I find nine and a half millions have been expended on the Quebec harbour since 1896. Adding that to the million and a half expenditure under consideration now, we have about eleven million, as the hon gentlemen from West York (Sir Henry Drayton) pointed out, and about six million are overdue for interest. I contend that, if the constitution of the board were a little different, if the port of Quebec were kept out of politics, and a permanent commission and permanent officers appointed to administer these affairs, it would be a great benefit to the country from the commercial aspect, and from the point of view of developing the port and the ocean traffic, inbound and outbound. It would be much better for the port of Quebec if Quebec city contributed something also and the port was developed by asking the commissioners to link the harbour up with the Quebec park system, with the Plains of Abraham Commission, another federal commission which is spending money, and the Immigration Department, and co-ordinate it all under one commission.
Part of the money is for facilities which the hon. minister points out. These terminal facilities may be badly needed, but they are not all what they should be, if the desire is to keep pace with the growth of the country.
There are some features of this proposition which I do not agree with. In the first place, the details are not given. What does "terminal facilities" mean; what does " equipment " mean in the resolution? In the second place, how is it that votes for Montreal and Quebec are being brought on now by special resolution, instead of being dealt with when the main estimates are before the House? There are other ocean ports. For instance, we have Vancouver and Victoria, where four and six million have been expended since 1896. Then we have Halifax and St. John. How is it they are not brought on by separate resolutions also? Then we have the ports of the cities of Toronto and Hamilton. The citizens of Toronto, with the government, are spending $26,000,000 or $28,000,000 to rebuild the port, and are only getting five or six millions from the government and are themselves spending about

Quebec Harbour
$21,000,000. Terminal facilities have been badly needed there. The city has an agreement signed by the harbour commission on one side and by the Canadian Pacific and the Grand Trunk on the other, to re-bulid the port, moving all the docks out into the bay a certain distance, and erect a station and viaduct, and provide terminals. The Government has been approached by the harbour commission and other bodies recently to ask the Grand Trunk Railway Company to carry out that agreement. Why is that port not dealt with by a separate resolution also? Is it because the province of Quebec is so hungry that they cannot wait for the main estimates? I would not like to say, and I do not say that that is the fact. I believe that all the harbours should be dealt with together, when the main estimates are brought down because I contend that what is good for the ports of Halifax, St. John and Montreal, is good for all the ports, and that those ports should be properly taken care of, with a view to expansion of business in the future, not only for ocean traffic, but for proper terminal facilities, to fit in with the National Railways and act as feeders for them.
It is in the public interest that the harbour of Quebec and other harbours should be kept out of politics, and that we should not remove the commissioners with every change of government. I have been on the harbour commission of Toronto since 1905-it was reorganized in 1911. It is a permanent commission. If we are to have proper development of a harbour, we must have continuity of management and control and a proper sale of bonds by tender. I say that the Minister of Finance should sell these bonds not by private sale, but by public tender. Toronto harbour sold two million by private sale and about fifteen million by tender. Instead of giving the bonds to one company, by private sale, tenders were openly granted. We opened up the door and we got about fifteen bids from Toronto, Philadelphia and New York. The public sale proved a good financial piece of business. We borrowed at from one-half of one to one and a half points better by public tender than by private sale. I submit the minister should call for tenders in reference to the bonds for Quebec harbour, and that the Government should annul all these commissions and co-ordinate the various expenditures of money on terminals in Quebec harbour and for the National railways, the Immigration Branch, the Public Works Department

and other facilities. I think the Harbour Commission should negotiate with the city of Quebec if they cannot make such an arrangement. There is the work on the Battlefields' Commission, the Quebec Parks Commission, and the work of making Quebec a city with proper boulevards and driveways. This work would create an industrial area where industries could be located with proper arrangements for terminal facilities in the way of docks, etc., such as they have in New York. You would have a large revenue from the industrial and recreation areas which would go a long way to help pay the fixed charges on the bonds of Quebec harbour instead of their being a drag on the country, with the result that the interest and the sinking fund charges would be met. Some development of this kind should be made, and, if it were made, I believe that in time Quebec port would meet its fixed charges. We are going to meet these fixed charges in Toronto from our revenues and pay the fixed charges out of revenue on the $17,000,000 which has thus far been expended, by developing the industrial area in Ashbridge's bay and the amusement areas at Sunnyside.
* I believe that if, instead of having politics in the Quebec Harbour Commission, they would change the principle and have a permanent non-political commission, they would meet with success. I represent , a Conservative city, but on the harbour commission of that city, when it was formed, we had two Liberals out of five, and they were good. We have no politics there, and the harbour improvements, from revenues, are going to pay for themselves. These improvements will not, in time, cost the taxpayer a cent. What has been done in Toronto should be done in Quebec as well.
I think the minister should give us some explanation as to why the late commissioners and officials were removed. Were they not good men? Did they not do good work? What was the reason for the change of the commission? This is not the only vote before the committee. The next vote will be for Montreal. A motion is also on the Order Paper for a vote of a million dollars for terminals for Montreal, and the Government are asked for two hundred thousand for a world's fair, and five millions for a bridge-Quebec is getting hungry. No doubt they are hungry. I think the minister should give us some explanation as to the future policy of the port of Quebec-the terminals and inbound and outbound, the rates to be col-

Quebec Harbour
lected, as to the change of the commission, and the broadening out of the commission as aforesaid.
In addition to that vote $23,000,000 was spent by the Government of Canada in deepening the channels between Quebec and Montreal, to give a deepwater channel to Montreal. I say every vote along those lines should be linked up-Quebec, Montreal and the depeening of the channel, from there to the Great Lakes. These deepwater channels should be extended to the head of the Great Lakes. We should have a declaration of policy along these lines. We have very little explanation about the port of Quebec. The Deep Waterways' Commission in their report deal with the future of the port of Quebec and the way it should be co-ordinated with the St. Lawrence scheme and I should like to hear from the minister his views on that subject. We would like to have the Government's views about the deepening of the channels from Quebec to Montreal and to the head of the lakes as recommended by the Deep Waterways' Commission.

I would submit to the Labour Department that if this clause goes through some provision should be inserted that any contract entered into under it should contain what is known as the "fair wage" clause. It has been found in other cities, where a provision of this kind has not been made, that contractors with the harbour commissioners disregard the ordinary fair wage clause, contending that they are not under contract with the Government but with the Commissioners. This happened in connection with the Vancouver harbour commission, and I therefore draw the attention of the Minister (Mr. Lapointe) , while we are on this subject, to the necessity for incorporating a fair wage clause in any contract made under the expenditure of this money.

My attention has already been called to this matter, and I shall certainly see that the fair wage clause shall be respected by the harbour commissioners of Quebec. I believe that contracts in connection with all subsidized works should contain a fair wage clause.

I should like some information from the minister with regard to a supplementary estimate brought down last year on the 4th day of June. The item then discussed read:
Amount required to pay the Park St. Charles Company, Limited, for land occupied by the
Quebec Harbour Commission, as per verdict of arbitrator, which verdict was later sustained by the Superior Court, in favour of the plaintiff company, $60,000.
I would also quote a part of the discussion that took place on that occasion on this matter. The first speaker, after the item had been introduced, was the hon. member for Maisonneuve (Mr. Lemieux), who said:
I object to the passing of this item. This is another land grab absolutely unjustifiable. It is a scandalous affair, and in the interest of my hon. friend the Minister of Finance I would ask him not to insist on the passing of this item. I remember the saying of an old cynic who was prominent in public life many years ago, that if at times he did purchase votes, at least he had the satisfaction of purchasing those votes with the people's money. This item is to make good the promises that were made during an election which has just taken place. The men who are interested in this land grab were most prominent in the election held in the county of Yamaska.
I shall not quote the whole of the hon. member's remarks, but I do wish to give his summing up of the matter. He proceeded :
I assert, Mr. Chairman, that this amount is not due. I know the value of land around that park, and it is an imposition on the good faith of the supporters of the Government to come before them with this demand in the dying hours of the session. The truth of the matter is that the country is being asked to pay the debts incurred in the Yamaska bye-election, because the men who are at the bottom of this land graft are the men who were sent into the constituency to interrupt my hon. friend from Quebec East and who canvassed the county in automobiles. Even if I have to stay here, I will not stand for this land graft, for it is a land graft. Ordinarily I support the city of Quebec, but as a taxpayer and as a representative of the people, I protest against any highway robbery from whatever quarter it comes.
The discussion was somewhat protracted, and further on the same hon. gentleman said:
When the next session comes-perhaps before -I will be in a position to establish to the right hon. gentleman and to Parliament that there has been fraud in this matter from beginning to end.
The then Prime Minister (Mr. Meighen) speaking on the question, is reported as follows:
We will expect the hon. gentleman to do it sooner than that. We would like to know, because if these people are entitled to their money they ought to have it. It is for him to establish by indisputable evidence before the department his charges of fraud and collusion in regard to this matter and we will provide the opportunity for him to do it.
Now, this was a pretty serious charge to make and if the Government haid consid-
Quebec Harbour

ered that there was no foundation for it they would not have withdrawn the item at that time. The Prime Minister of that day declared that a tribunal would he established to take evidence on the matter and ascertain whether or not the charge was true. We have had no indication since as to whether any action has been taken in the matter, and before we go further I should like the minister to say what has been done.

I understand that no
steps have been taken with regard to the Park St. Charles matter. As my hon. friend knows, this was an appropriation in the supplementary estimates. It was not voted last year, and I do not know whether it will be voted this year. However, that is not strictly relevant to the matter immediately under consideration.

My hon.
friend's recollection is at fault. Action was taken. The hon. member who made the charge was invited to go before that investigation and submit his proof, but he took the stand that he did not approve of that kind of 'investigation. He thought that the matter should be investigated by a parliamentary committee.

Possibly; but I have no doubt that the Chairman would like me to point out that all I am doing is answering statements made from the governmental benches on the invitation of my hon. friend to my left (Mr. Caldwell). If the whole discussion be ruled out, I do not mind.
I merely said that the Government had taken no steps in the direction of paying the amount.

The hon.
gentleman was referring to what had been done to implement the promise that an investigation would be held.

No; I was pointing
out that we have not taken any steps.
He was speaking of this Government.

this Government is doing nothing one way or the other. I do not know whether they will bring on the investigation.

I think we should have
some reply to the rather serious objections registered against the grant by the hon. member for West York (Sir Henry Drayton). Personally, I want to preserve an open mind in regard to the matter, but this is a time when we cannot afford to give away any money which we need for other purposes, and there are some facts in connection with this matter which, I think, need clearing up. As my hon. friend
knows, this resolution is only the first stage in this legislation. It was my intention to give full explanations later on, but if my hon. friend so desires, I am quite willing to answer any questions which he would like to ask me now. My hon. friend from West York is quite correct when he says that this has not so far been a paying investment. The hon. member should not call it an investment at all. It is, of course, an investment in that it is intended for the general advancement of the country in developing a national port which is essential to the business of the Dominion. But as regards its being a paying proposition in the way of returning interest, it has never been considered in the light of an investment, and should not be so considered. My hon. friend from Toronto (Mr. Church) is a nice fellow and I should not like to have any difficulty with him. He has invited me to go to his place and has promised me the time of my life.

Will he introduce you
to Judge Cohen?

But I may tell him
that Quebec would like to be in the same position as Toronto; it would also like to get money from the Government and give nothing in return. Such money is not considered in anyway whatever as being due

either in the way of capital or of interest by the city of Toronto or the Harbour Commission of that city. Even this year there is an appropriation in the public works estimates for the Toronto harbour improvements, and it is not provided that the harbour commissioners shall pay one cent of interest on the money contributed by the country. The conditions are not the same in any way whatever, and I think my hon. friend was wrong in using such rather strong language and saying that we in Quebec are hungry. At least, as oiie of my hon. friends on the other side told me, if we are hungry we are not thirsty.
Last year for the first time five million bushels of wheat were shipped from Quebec I may inform my hon. friend from West York (Sir Henry Drayton). We are in communication with the railway companies with a view to developing this export traffic, and the prospects are encouraging. But these advances are not for the purpose of developing or improving the grain facilities at the elevator there, except for a small amount of $20,000, necessary to complete the elevator. All the other items are either for the purpose of completing work already started or to make repairs which are absolutely necessary to preserve what has been already constructed.
The harbour commission of Quebec intended to build a cold storage warehouse, and they asked for $500,000 more than the Government has agreed to advance. We thought this was a new work that could very well wait, and we told them that their request would be reconsidered when the necessity for such a warehouse was more urgent than it appears to be at the present time. I have here a report of the movement of vessels in and out of the port of Quebec for 1919 and 1920; the report of the operations for 1920 and 1921 has not yet been received by the department. The movement of vessels inwards and outwards for 1920 as compared with 1919 shows an increase of 69 vessels, as follows:
Inwards: 1920, 460; 1919, 331.
Outwards: 1920, 214; 1919, 274.
I think these advances are necessary, Mr. Chairman; indeed, we would not ask parliament to sanction them if they were not absolutely necessary at the present time to preserve from destruction works already constructed, and to furnish the shipping accommodation required at this port.
My hon. friend from West York seems to think that no vessels are using the port of Quebec. What would the bigger liners do if they had not this port to use on the St. Lawrence route? Those liners do not go to Montreal, despite the money that has been spent, as my hon. friend complained, in deepening the channel between the two ports, because the underwriters do not think it would be safe for them to incur the risks involved. If any further explanations are required, I shall be happy to furnish them.
