335,303	17Mr. JOHNSON	(Moosejaw) : Mr.	Chairman, anything I have	to	say on this	resolution is more by way of securing information than argument for or against it. Part of the information I sought has already been supplied by the minister (Mr. Lapointe), supplemented by the remarks of the exMinister of Finance (Sir Henry Drayton). It was not clear in my mind whether the moneys mentioned in this resolution were capital expenditure on behalf of the Dominion Government, or a loan to the Quebec harbour commissioners, repayable with interest. I rather gather-the minister will correct me if I am wrong-that it is a loan to the Quebec harbour commissioners with very little prospect of repayment either of principal or interest. Consequently we may just as well take it for what it really is-capital expenditure by the people of Canada generally to develop this particular port.
Were its development at the present juncture sufficiently urgent and important to warrant that expenditure in my opinion, it would have my support; but I wonder if such is the case. We have been told repeatedly during the present session that the one thing we must keep constantly before our minds is economy in the expenditure of public moneys. A week ago, in company with other members, I visited the port of Quebec for the first time, and I am free to confess I was very much impressed with the ample shipping facilities the harbour
Quebec Harbour

commissioners have in their wonderful port, and the great opportunities for expansion. I know the hospitality of our friends from Quebec was too genuine an article to be sullied with any commercial or mercenary motives; any information furnished to us was received in the spirit in which it was tendered, and on my part at least I found it very valuable.
The harbour commissioners, as was pointed out, have remarkable facilities- and a grievance. But if I interpreted the representations aright, the grievance took more the character of it being impossible to secure the volume of business which the existing facilities were able to handle. I gathered that what would help the harbour more than anything else would be that traffic from the national roads should be so increased that the facilities would be used to capacity, which they are not now. When that stage comes it will be time enough in my opinion to consider the further expansion of those facilities. If that contention is right, it is so closely related to railway rates that we can scarcely consider the one without the other. I am not going to discuss railway rates as a concrete subject to-day; we had enough of that yesterday; but we who live in the interior and ship bulk products across the continent to the Atlantic ports, have been taught, and have come to belive, that all-rail routes, to the Atlantic seaboard points can never hope to compete with rail and water routes. Now, that principle may be subject to variation; but I wondered when this was brought to my attention whether, in that portion of the year when heavy commodities such as grain go by rail to the Atlantic seaboard, the port of Quebec could not be given the benefit of such freight rates on the National Transcontinental as would enable it to compete with other ports which are only a little closer to the interior than Quebec is, and not nearly so close to the European countries. I thought something might be done on behalf of the port of Quebec. Then, I had hoped to get some information as to the volume of traffic which is now offering. I did not wish to compare the various ports, but it was evident that the port of Quebec must always be our chief Canadian port in the summer season for passenger traffic, package freight, and shipments which must move hurriedly into the interior. Quebec has, it seems to me, adequate facilities for that kind of business.

Now, Montreal is, after all, the nearest point reached by rail from the interior to tidewater or to open ocean ports. Are the facilities at the port of Montreal-and I am asking simply for information, because I do not know-adequate to handle the business at present offering? The minister will perhaps answer that question later. I hope I would not be considered as taking a parochial view if I spoke of the relation of this subject to western problems, but after all, we cannot have the one without the other. What is the use of terminal facilities if you do not have adequate facilities at the initial points of shipment, and vice versa? I notice also, on page 35 of the estimates, that items which have been referred to by the member for North Toronto (Mr. Church), aggregating almost $2,000,000, for the improvement of various ports and harbour facilities, are chargeable to capital. And here is an item of $1,500,000 which, taking the information supplied by the minister a few minutes ago, I cannot look upon as other than a capital expenditure, in effect at least. So that we run up an item of $3,500,000 to furnish terminal facilities for the shipment of our products to European countries. In other words, we take care of the outlet for traffic originating in the interior, though we neglect- and I think I am speaking correctly, Mr. Chairman-we neglect the development of those facilities which are necessary to the gathering of that business. Many of us from western Canada have been most persistent in our representations to the Minister of Railways for branch line extensions, and we have been impressed by his argument that these works could not be undertaken owing to lack of money and to the necessity for economy. Well, we have taken him at his word; but it seems rather hopeless that we should be asked to vote large sums for the equipment and development of terminal facilities when we neglect the feeders which are so essential if the fullest use is to be made of the facilities which are already at our disposal. Much as I appreciate the situation as respects the harbour of Quebec, as well as other harbours mentioned in the estimates, and much as I would like to see them develop and made the best harbours in the world, I cannot see my way clear to support a vote for these improvements so long as, on the ground of economy, extensions and feeders back in the interior are left to wait for better times.

Quebec Harbour

I am most anxious to see Quebec become one of our great national ports. Perhaps there is some sentiment mixed up with my desire in that respect; I always look upon Quebec as the ancient capital of the land, and I believe that nature intended that it would become one of the great, if not the greatest, of our summer ports. But the statement which has been given to the committee this afternoon by the hon. member for West York (Sir Henry Drayton) almost staggers one when one attempts to consider the proposal now before the committee for the appropriation of another million and a half dollars. I can well remember the 4th of May in the year 1901, when a committee of the House was invited to go to the city of Quebec to examine the harbour, and I see hon. members in the House now who, with myself, went to Quebec on that occasion and had a most enjoyable day. History has been repeating itself, because I believe that a week or ten days ago another more limited committee went to Quebec with a view to looking over the harbour. Well, twenty years ago we started on fairly liberal expenditure in regard to the port of Quebec. We were very optimistic in those days as to the prospect for the future and felt very sure of the results which would be obtained. But, as I say, I was staggered this afternoon to hear the statement made by the member for West York as to the results which have been achieved after an experience of twenty odd years in connection with expenditures at that port. The hon. member for Moosejaw (Mr. Johnson) has, I think, properly put the matter before the committee; we must look upon this outlay as capital expenditure, not as a loan. An ex-Finanee Minister of this country informs the House that our expenditures under this head in past years, amounting to about $11,000,000, have practically been written off as an asset. It is, then, a capital expenditure from which we have little hope of obtaining anything, either by way of principal or by way of interest. There is little doubt in my mind that if we spend another million and a half as proposed by this resolution we need not look for either the return of capital or the payment of interest. Now, the result in Montreal, I am informed, has been quite different. Montreal has developed into a very busy port. The bonds of the harbour commissioners there are saleable; the interest upon them is paid to the government; they are considered a fairly high-class investment. I am told also that the same
thing applies to Vancouver, but for some reason or other it does not apply to Quebec. During the past two years I have visited the city of Quebec, particularly the military district there, on two or three occasions, and incidentally I have had interviews with some of the citizens in regard to the question of the harbour. I must say the impression I gained was just the impression given to the committee this afternoon by my hon. friend from Moose-jaw. The complaint of the citizens of Quebec was not that the harbour facilities were inadequate; the impression left on my mind was that they had one of the best equipped harbours in the country or on the continent, but the regret was that there was no business to be done. The complaint was directed entirely to the fact that the business coming over the National Transcontinental Railway did not reach the city of Quebec.
The complaint was a complaint of freight rates. They complained of a rate which they said discriminated against the city of Quebec, and my information on those occasions was that if a proper adjustment of freight rates was made, the port of Quebec would be one of the busiest in the Dominion. Well, the freight rate question has not yet been adjusted. From information I gathered, and from anything I saw, I certainly formed the opinion that the facilities were there far in advance of the requirements. The facilities were there for a trade enormously in advance of any trade they are doing at the port of Quebec at the present time, or can hope to do within a reasonable period irt the future. If that be so, would it not be idle for this House to advance another $1,500,000 at the present time?
I view the matter this way. I do not want by my voice or my my vote to interrupt the progress or development of that port. I want to see it go ahead, but at the same time would it be a wise thing to expend $1,500,000 under the conditions as we know them to-day in this House? Is not this a matter that can well wait for future consideration until we see what is going to be done about railway rates, railway schedules, and the like? If the conditions as they exist to-day are to continue in regard to railway traffic, there are more facilities at the port of Quebec now than will be used for many, many years. If a change takes place, the facilities there to-day will take care of a very largely increased business for a number of years to come. Then, cannot we allow this present
Quebec Harbour

proposal to stand until the trade figures warrant additional expenditure, until we can see some hope of getting something back, or at least of having an investment of some value to the Dominion of Canada.
Criticism has been made against the city of Toronto. It has been suggested that the harbour expenditures there have been in the nature of gifts to the city ox Toronto. I think it is something to the credit of the city of Toronto, a proof of their progressive spirit, that while the Government has contributed, and contributed on a fairly liberal scale, to harbour improvements in that city, the citizens themselves have also contributed very much more liberally. For every dollar that this Government has spent on harbour improvements in Toronto, I am told that the citizens have spent five or six dollars of their own money. I do not believe the city of Quebec has ever made a contribution of any kind towards its harbour, not for many years, at all events. It may originally have done so, but in the last twenty or twenty-five years there has been no municipal expenditure on the part of Quebec. So long as we view that port solely as a national port, I do not know that the citizens of Quebec should be called to make any expenditure, but these improvements are undoubtedly a convenience and an asset to the city. They are a help to the citizens; the more trade that is done there, the better for the city of Quebec, but during the last twenty or twenty-five years, I believe I am correct in saying', the citizens of Quebec have not paid anything towards their harbour, while the citizens of Toronto have taxed themselves to the tune of something like $20,000,000 for harbour improvements there. If the money must be spent now, if the minister can make out a case for this expenditure at the present time, I shall not stand in the way of it, but I must say that in my judgment this expenditure might stand for one or two or three or five years, until we see some business in sight at that port which is not there at the present time.

I am really surprised to hear the hon. member state that the citizens of Quebec have never made any contribution towards their harbour, or any sacrifice to obtain what is due to them. Let me remind the hon. gentleman that on many occasions in this House I have had the honour to quote from the written agreement between the federal govern-

ment and the city of Quebec, by which the Government bound themselves to make certain improvements and construct certain works at that port. I would remind the hon. gentleman that the attitude he has taken to-day with regard to this expenditure is not the attitude that his late chief, the Right Hon. Sir Robert Borden, and his colleagues took when they were entertained at a banquet at the Chateau Frontenac in the city of Quebec in 1913. On that occasion the Prime Minister of that day told the citizens of Quebec that there was nothing too good for them, and that the pledges of the government in respect to the port of Quebec would be fulfilled. I would also remind the hon. gentleman of the statements made by Sir Robert Borden when he came down to inaugurate the works at the port of Quebec. He stated then that moneys would be provided for the Quebec Harbour Commission, and that the proper equipment would be provided.
We have provided all that.

Is the hon. gentleman really able to state what has been done by the Quebec Harbour Commission lately? The promises which the late government made of improvements to the port of Quebec have never been fulfilled. I do not know of any solid promise which was made by the late government and the gov-* ernment of Sir Robert Borden to the city of Quebec which has been fulfilled. Millions of dollars have been promised the city for docks, wharves, grain elevators, and all kinds of improvements.
They have got all that.

We have got a
grain elevator, but it is only a small one, and not of the capacity we should have in the city of Quebec. An elevator of the proper capacity in that city would be a benefit to the country as a whole. Our elevator has a capacity of 2,000,000 or
3.000.	000 bushels.

A capacity of
2.000.	000 bushels.

We should have an elevator with a capacity of at least
10.000.	000 bushels. That is what we were promised.
How much grain passed through that elevator last year?

About 5,000,000
bushels.

Quebec Harbour

If we had the proper facilities, and the proper freight rates, so that the grain from the West could be brought to the city of Quebec, if we had the tariff of twenty cents a bushel which was promised, the business done would be very much larger and several millions of dollars would be saved to the people of the West. The country as a whole would benefit from the application of such a tariff, but even if we had the traffic, we have not the port facilities to handle it at the present time. I am delighted to see that the Minister of Marine has placed a sum in the estimates to enable proper equipment to be provided for the harbour of Quebec. But even that amount is only a small contribution towards carrying out the promise made to the citizens of Quebec subsequent to 1911, a promise which has never been fulfilled.

I would like to point out to the hon. member (Mr. Lavig-ueur) that he is making a mistake in saying that nothing has been done. I am afraid some people will think we did a great deal too much for Quebec. It was thought a great deal could be done for "the fair city of Quebec" and we did hope to do a great deal. I would remind my hon. friend that the carrying out of that intention resulted in an expenditure of three and a half millions on the Quebec harbour in 1913; an expenditure of $2,000,000 in 1914; and an expenditure of $1,491,-(00 in 1917.

The statement I
made was that nothing has been done to carry out the written contract entered into by the late government. My hon. friend (Mr. Guthrie) a few minutes ago stated that Quebec had never contributed anything toward the contemplated improvements in that city. I would point out that the city of Quebec has given property worth over $2,000,000 in order to secure a proper equipment for the port. Quebec gave up the Champlain market which was a property valued at over $2,000,000, and what did it get in return for that surrender? The late government built a terminal station on that site which is a disgrace to the city, and worth at the utmost only some twenty-five or thirty thousand dollars. Under the Laurier regime the contract was awarded for the erection of a station on the Champlain market site to cost over $1,000,000. When the Borden government came in they cancelled that contract, and instead of giving us the
magnificent edifice planned by Sir Wilfrid Laurier they erected a miserable building which they thought was good enough for the citizens of Quebec.

It seems to me that during the years of the war period, and during the years when prosperity reigned, we acquired habits of extravagance. It is not easy to escape from these habits, but I believe the time has come when instead of talking in terms of millions when contemplating expenditures we shall have to be more economical and speak in the language of thousands. While formerly we talked in language that is parochial, looking after our own interests in our own particular section, we are now compelled to look at matters from a national viewpoint. Much of the discussion that has taken place to-day would indicate that the gravity of the financial problem confronting the Government at the present time has not been fully realized. I am not going to devote much time in repeating what has been already said, and said in better terms than I can employ. I would say, however, in reply to my hon. friend from Quebec (Mr. Lavigueur) in regard to Sir Robert Borden's reported statement a short time ago "that nothing was too good for the city of Quebec," that we are now living in other days. Many great changes have taken place since the time to which my hon. friend has alluded; and that whether we want to or not we are compelled to-day to prune down our estimates. Many of us thought that drastic cuts in the public expenditure could be made. Now we begin to realize that trade would be so upset and the inconvenience would be so great in consequence that ws cannot go to extremes in the matter. But there is no doubt that there must be a paring down of expenditures.
There is one phase of this matter I would like to deal with particularly. I believe that many members of this House and many people in the country, consider the economic depression-and I refer more particularly to the state of agriculture-is such that all that is necessary is to have a little patience and things will right themselves in a very short time. I believe the people who entertain that view are very much mistaken. Let me indulge in a little retrospect. Many of those hon. members who have farmed in the West can remember the days wThen land on the prairies ready for the plough was purchased at $6 an acre-yes $2.50 an acre, the very best land that lies out of doors. That land was
Quebec Harbour

absolutely free from weeds; all we had to do was to scratch the surface and it would yield a crop. In those days of prosperity we could stand a great many burdens, and we did support many and did not raise much complaint respecting them. We hardily counted the cost. We knew we were carrying great burdens, but we were living in times of prosperity and felt able to stand them. Now the time has come when that land is not so productive as it was. During the last twenty years it has decreased in production to the extent of six bushels per acre. My remarks, of course, apply to the prairie provinces. The cost of production has now become very high, and, in a very few words, I will give you my reason why there has been such an enhancement in cost and why we cannot get back to normal conditions without drastic efforts on the part of the federal government. The time came when competition was set aside by some of those engaged in manufacturing articles for our use, but at first we thought we could stand it. I will not say that the manufacturers of farming implements were the first to inaugurate this proceeding but I know they were among the first. Let me illustrate what took place by a concrete case. I said to a man who was a manufacturer and seller of sheaf loaders "That article should not cost $500; it should not cost more than $250." He replied "We do not figure the selling price according to the cost at all. We believe that the man who is threshing grain will regard it as worth his while to pay $500 rather than be without it. Therefore we charge him $500." Now that sort of thing has taken place all along the line. All the various interests have organized even down to labour. When labour organized and demanded a high wage, the time arrived when it was absolutely impossible for us to continue to pay that high wage any longer. During last fall, because of this economic depression, the loan companies took this action. They were not able to collect their loans or the interest. Of course matured loans must be renewed. They were renewed in many cases, not at 8 per cent, but 9 per cent.
THE CHAIRMAN: This discussion as to loan companies in the West can hardly be relevant to this particular issue. I observe the hon. member is drawing a comparison, but I think he is going a little beyond the length of address he is entitled to give in drawing that comparison.

I was only mentioning
that as an incident, not dealing fully with it, but merely wishing to show that conditions surrounding agriculture are such that, unless economy is practised by the Government, so as to lessen the burden the country is carrying at the present time, no grain or other freight would go to the port of Quebec or any other port. An effort has been made to show that an expenditure on the port of Quebec would be wise if the railways could be persuaded to carry the freight east, instead of letting it go by water. This, it seems to me, is an effort to make water run uphill. The freight will go very much cheaper by water than by rail, and I see no good reason why any effort should be made to cause it to go by rail, in order that the port of Quebec may be built up. Considering that about $11,000,000 has already been spent on this port, and the amount of traffic passing through it has been very small, it certainly seems to me very unwise that another million and a half should be spent.
Reference has been made to the necessity for branch lines. A few days ago I received a letter from some gentlemen, who are interested in a branch line that has been partly built for some two or three years. Ties have been laid, and I believe a large quantity of rails is ready to be laid down, and these gentlemen said "If the Government is not ready to complete this railway at this time, we farmers of this district would like to complete it ourselves, and be paid for our work by way of freight on the produce, principally grain, that will be carried on the railway." At the present time one reason why this branch line should be built is because a great deal of the grain that would go to the Government railways is now going by the Canadian Pacific railway. When many districts require the expenditure of money that
5 p.m. will bring good returns in order to help a basic industry like agriculture, I ask if it would be wise to consider spending another million and. a half on the port of Quebec. It sems to me not.	.
You may think, Mr. Chairman, that I have wandered a little from the subject, but I have not spent very much of the time of this House in discussing any matter. If it costs $2,000 an hour, as some have figured, to talk to this House, I believe other members have been greater sinners than I have. Let me say to the cities of the pro-

Quebec Harbour
vince of Quebec, and to all other cities, that it is well that they should get together and consider this difficult problem in which Canada is placed, because the reaction has already set in. Manufacturing concerns and the railways are suffering; in fact, almost every industry in Canada is suffering. If hon. gentlemen stop to think for a little while, I think they will see why. You can lay such burdens on the basic industries of Canada that their purchasing power will be impaired, and that is what has taken place during the recent years and months. Those engaged in farming-and I suppose many others are similarly placed -are unable to purchase as they used to. They have to cut their purchases to the very bone, and when they cannot purchase, naturally those who are manufacturing have to close their shops. There is unemployment; the railways have not the traffic to carry and there is impoverishment all along the line. I think it would be well, for that reason, that those who think of spending money in Government work that could very well wait for a year or two, should take that fact into consideration. If they would wait a few years until the basic industries get on their feet again, and a certain degree of prosperity returns, then if the million, or two or three million, is required to improve the port of Quebec, or Montreal, or even Toronto-which, as a matter of fact, has been very persistent in its demands-I think you would find those who are engaged in agriculture would not be backward in supporting their demands. We are not looking at things in a narrow way, but rather in a broad way. We see that a reaction has taken place and that there is no chance of a return of prosperity in Canada until the basic industries receive the consideration to which they are entitled because of their importance. I ask the Government to give consideration to that point.
Who are the Quebec harbour commisioners at the present time?
Mr. Power, Mr. Gau-vin and General Tremblay.	*
What was the minister's idea in changing the harbour commissioners?
To form a new board, in order that there might be co-operation in the work of the commission.
What reason had the minister to think that with the old board there would not be co-operation?
My right hon. friend knows what the old harbour commission was, and he was anxious to have the documents of the House, and they have been laid on the table.
They give no reason.
I am going to give reasons. I do not think anybody could accuse me of being a very bitter political partisan and, I think, if I have any reproach laid against me, it is quite the contrary.
I never heard the contrary reproach.
The hon. gentleman is not in the right camp to hear that report.

I think political patronage must be eliminated, as far as possible. But what were the conditions there? The chairman of the harbour commission was a friend of mine personally. He was a gallant soldier and did his duty for his country. Unfortunately, he is dead now, and it is a delicate matter to speak of him in any way, but I am sure my right hon. friend will not consider that I am speaking disparagingly of him when I say that he was a strong partisan of my right hon. friend and of hisjparty. That was right; I have no complaint whatever to make in that regard. But he was the owner, the publisher and the manager of a newspaper in the city of Quebec called The Quebec Chronicle, which is perhaps the strongest political journal in that province.
Tory.

The chairman of the
harbour commission continued as publisher, manager and owner of that newspaper after the new cabinet had come into office, and almost every day there were editorials in that newspaper not only against the Government, but directed against the Minister of Marine in particular. I have nothing to complain about concerning any such criticisms coming from any citizen, but my right hon. friend will admit that this was a condition of things that could not be tolerated. The chairman of the harbour commission is not, perhaps, a civil servant. If he were he would have been instantly dismissed for offensive political partisanship, under the Civil Service Act. But he is more than a civil servant; he is even more than a deputy minister, because there is less control over him. He is the administrator
Quebec Harbour

of the harbour, and surely he must have some confidence in the Minister of Marine and Fisheries, as the minister must likewise have confidence in his officer. There could he no co-operation if the two were distrustful of each other so far as political questions are concerned. That was the only reason for my having asked for his resignation; and I may say that everyone expected it. The matter was not criticised by the friends of my right hon. friend in Quebec. The new Harbour Board is considered by all the citizens of Quebec as a good business body. They were entertained last night by all the business men of the city, Conservatives as well as Liberals, and I think that my right hon. friend will concede that it was impossible to act otherwise under the circumstances. At 'all events, I thought I did the right thing. I could not do otherwise, and I oifer no apology whatever in this matter. If there is anything wrong about what I did, I must confess that I am an unrepentant sinner and certainly deserve all that may be coming to me in consequence of my action.

What was the offence
of Mr. Gravel? Was he a criminal in the sense of being a Conservative too?

Three or four years
ago, when Sir David Watson was appointed chairman of the Harbour Commission in Quebec, Mr. Pennington, who was a member of the board, did not resign. The former government, properly as I think, thought that when the board had to be reorganized and the chairman had severed his connection with it, it was necessary to appoint a new board altogether. My right hon. friend (Mr. Meighen) shakes his head, but I know that that is what was done three years ago, and it was done this year also. It was thought advisable to retain one of. the three former commissioners, and General Tremblay was retained. There was no question about political partisanship on his part. He was not the owner of a newspaper carrying on an offensive campaign against the Government, and nothing concerning him deserves criticism.
Are any of the present appointees related to the minister?

Not in the slightest
degree. My right hon. friend has been utterly misinformed.

I did not say I was
informed at all. Now, I take a different view altogether from that of the minister

of his conduct in this regard, and if I may interpret his own heart at this moment, I am not sure that he has fully confessed his own sense of his conduct.
I certainly have.

At the time Sir David
Watson was appointed, one member of the board was asked to retire. As I understand, it has been the custom to have two French Canadians and one Protestant member on the board, and it was in order to maintain the two French Canadian members that the other one was asked to re-' tire. That is what the late government did; it was not because of any political reason. On the contrary, so far as I know, the man who was asked to retire was a friend of the Government. But this government comes into office; it finds Sir David Watson with almost five years of service in Europe, service recognized by the appointment of him as Chairman of the Harbour Board. It finds him eminently successful in his office; it also finds Brigadier-General Tremblay in office, a man also of some length of service in the war. It finds him successful as well. It finds in office Mr. Gravel, who represented particularly the Levis side of the river on the board. And almost the first act of the minister is to write letters to these gentlemen and ask for their resignations. I have before me a copy of the letter which the minister wrote to Sir David Watson. Let me read it:
Dear Sir David Watson :
Since asuming the direction of the Marine and Fisheries Department, I have given consideration to the policies that should, in my judgment, he adopted by the Government with reference to the administration of the harbours of Montreal and Quebec. In order that the Government and myself should have a free hand in the creation of an administration in sympathy with those public policies, the former Commissioners from the harbour of Montreal voluntarily tendered their resignation.
I have not yet asked for the correspondence in that connection.
You will, I am sure, appreciate that the adoption of a similar policy respecting the harbour of Quebec is eminently desirable in the public interest. I have therefore to respectfully request you to forward to me your resignation as president of the Quebec Harbour Commissioners, so that the Government may be enabled with as little delay as possible to organise an administration along the lines heretofore indicated. I am forwarding a similar request to the other members of the Commission.
The request goes to General Tremblay and to Mr. Gravel. I have the reply which Sir David Watson sent, as brought down

Quebec Harbour
by the minister. It will be noted that the reason given by the minister for requesting the resignation of these gentlemen is in order that the Government may be free to appoint men in sympathy with those public policies which the Government con->
templates in respect of the harbour of Quebec, without the slightest information as to whether or not Sir David Watson was in sympathy with those public policies. That is what the minister said in his letter. Without any intimation to Sir David Watson as to what those public policies were-and I suppose we are getting them now-the minister assumed, that he was opposed to them, and on that ground demanded the resignation of as gallant an officer as ever served this or any other country. I shall read Sir David Watson's reply and leave it to the House as to where the honours of the argument lay after the minister had received it:
Quebec, February lOith, 1922.
Dear Sir,-This "will acknowledge yours of the 7th instant, in which you request me to forward my resignation as President of the Quebec Harbour Commission, arnd also note that you are forwarding a similar request to the other members of the Commission.
You state that you have given consideration to the policies that should, in your judgment, be adopted by the Government with reference to the administration of the Harbours of Montreal and Quebec, and point out that in order that the Government and yourself should have a free hand in the creation of an administration in sympathy with those public policies, the former Commissioners for the Harbour of Montreal voluntarily tender their resignations.
But when you go on to say that I will, you are sure, appreciate that the adoption of a similar policy respecting the harbour of Quebec is eminently desirable in the public interest, I fail to follow you. Since you have never enlightened me as to what these policies are that should, in your judgment, be adopted by the Government with regard to the harbour of Quebec, and have made no attempt whatever to ascertain my view's relative thereto, I am at a loss to know by what right you can assume in advance that my administration would not be fully sympathetic to the public policies to which you allude.
It will be a surprise, not only to myself but to the Citizens of Quebec, if you have any other policy in View than that of securing a maximum of business for the harbour, without prejudice to the legitimate claims of other Canadian ports, and of administering its affairs in general with efficiency and economy. With such a policy I am and have always been in complete sympathy; as evidence of which I may point out that for a great number of years, prior to my appointment, the Quebec Commission was administered at a considerable loss annually, due to lack of business in the port. Since my administration as Chairman, however, this deficit has been converted into a surplus as per extract from Official Auditor's report, handed in last week as follows:
"The revenue statement show's a marked improvement on the previous period, the gross deficit of $65,221.96 of last year being converted this year into a surplus of $52,020.74 showing a betterment of $117,242.70.
"Operating expenditures have been reduced from $387,619 to $335,303, a gain of $52,316. All items show a reduction except the 'Elevators' which against an increase in operating expenses of $22,322, show an improvement of $71,120 in revenue.'*
I was appointed to the chairmanship of the Quebec Harbour Commission in 1920, not by reason of services rendered to the late government or of sympathy with iits policies-so far as the harbour is concerned I never hesitated to urge its requirements and its rights-but for the same reason as my fellow-commissioner, Brigadier-General Tremblay: in recognition of five years of continuous war service in France, in the interest of the people of Canada.
In this connection, I assuredly cannot agree with your policy of treatment of returned men as Illustrated by your request for the resignations of Brigadier-Generar Tremblay and myself, and I further disagree with your policy if it is not directed towards the same satisfactory results as I have already been able to obtain, and which appears in the official Auditor's report quoted herein.
But above all I have no desire, nor would it be possible for me to co-operate with an administration whose policies appear from your letter to be so utterly at variance with the most elementary principles of justice and honour, and my resignation is herewith tendered in accordance with your request, to take effect at the end of the month.
Yours truly,
D. Watson,
Major-General, K.O., formerly commanding 4th Canadian Division.
Brigadier Tremblay tendered his resignation. I do not know what may have transpired between him and the minister, but the brigadier, being a consistent Liberal appointed by the late government, was reappointed by this Government. Mr. Gravel, who had been appointed to the port of Levis, was requested to hand in his resignation, which was accepted, and he also was effectually dismissed.
Sir David Watson's offence, according to my hon. friend, was that he was the owner of the Quebec Chronicle. It is true he was the owner of the majority stock of the Quebec Chronicle. It is true that the Quebec Chronicle supported the late government, and has always supported the Liberal-Conservative party. I want to know if the holding of majority stock or control of a newspaper supporting the late government is a bar to the holding of office as a harbour commissioner under this Government. Did the minister speak to me?

I was telling my hon. friend for George Etienne Cartier (Mr. Quebec Harbour

Jacobs) that Sir David Watson was not only the owner of the majority stock, hut he was general manager of the paper. The paper was published under his sole control.

Assuming he was general manager of the paper, did that interfere with the performance of his duties as harbour commissioner? It did not appear to. The duties of that office were performed more successfully by him than they had been performed by any one before.
His other duty was to attack this administration every morning for breakfast.

Very well. In the city of Quebec only one of the four or five papers is supporting the late government. A policy of purchase of antagonistic papers has been carried on by the friends of the hon. gentleman.
Name them.

I take the name of a paper right beside us-L'Evenement.	I
did not have to go far, did I?
Let those speak who know.

But where the attempt to purchase fails the big stick is applied, and the owner of the majority stock in the one remaining Conservative paper of the great city of Quebec is exposed to summary dismissal at the hands of my hon. friend though he was commander of the 4th Canadian Division for four years in France, and one of the most gallant men that this or any other country ever sent to the front. What offence did Mr. Gravel commit? I did not hear. The only offence he committed that I know of was to hold the office that the hon. minister wanted to fill with one of his friends. Everything the minister has advanced to-day, yes, many times in much stronger form, would be applicable to every case of political patronage the grossest that the country could conceive of; he could defend every case of patronage with the language he has employed this afternoon. Yes, patronage is bad enough, and I know how the minister is hankering to get back to it in all its various forms, but patronage as applied against the holding of offices that have been filled successfully by returned men is the most indefensible form of patronage.
Nor is this the only case to which it has been applied; there are many such cases throughout the country, reference to which has been made in questions put upon the
[Mr. Lapointe. |
Order Paper. But this is the most conspicuous one-a demand for resignation on a ground that is so manifestly indefensible and untenable that I am surprised the minister would put it forward. He had not the least reason to expect that Sir David Watson would change the political allegiance of his journal-a journal whose circulation was naturally with those of sympathetic views to itself. Sir David Watson personally was not in any sense active in the management of the Quebec Chronicle. He attended to his duties as harbour commissioner just as assiduously as he attended to his duties as general of our 4th Division in France; that was his conduct in office. Sir David Watson by his services to this country merited better treatment, and might have expected better treatment, at the hands of a generous foe. I may say that in correspondence received by myself from one of his friends, I am informed that the treatment accorded Sir David Watson was very severely felt by himself as unjust, cruel and ungrateful. To quote the last sentence of the letter:
I personally do not consider it too much to say that what the Huns failed to do the Liberals succeeded in accomplishing-killing him.

There are
some rules that apply to ordinary courtesy, and my hon. friend ought to know them.

The hon. gentleman
had better hold his own followers to that rule.

I have nothing to complain of concerning what my right hon. friend has done or said; it is like him, absolutely. He cannot induce me to say anything against the late Sir David Watson. The committee understands how delicate the subject is under the circumstances, so I will confine myself to stating again that I think no minister of the Crown, on whatever side of politics he may be, can, in his capacity as head of a department, co-operate with a deputy minister or the chairman of a board under his jurisdiction when these officials are assailing each other every morning in the newspapers, politically or otherwise. It would simply be stupidity to take any other course than was taken, and were I placed again in the same position I would act exactly as I did.
Now, my right hon. friend, in his very insinuating way, has said that he does not know about the commissioners of Montreal because he has not yet moved for the correspondence. Let me tell him that as soon as this Government took office the harbour commissioners of Montreal sent in their resignations. They did it in a very courteous way, and they were pleased to welcome the new commissioners who were appointed by this Government.
Did not the chairman of that board previously resign to become a candidate in St. Antoine?

The chairman had resigned to become a candidate for my right hon. friend in St. Antoine, and the two other commissioners resigned as soon as this Government took office. The Montreal Gazette, which is a respectable organ of my right hon. friend and has always been a Conservative newspaper, had something to say about that. The Gazette certainly does not share the opinion of my right hon. friend as to the co-operation which should exist between the Government or the Minister of Marine and Fisheries and the harbour commission of any port. Here is what the Montreal Gazette said in an editorial in its issue of February 1, entitled "The Harbour Board," in which it welcomed the appointments made by the Government:
The office of Hai-bor Commissioner has always been political in the sense that its occupants come and go with the changing governments at Otitawa, and in view of the intfimate relation between the port and the Government there can be no objection to this procedure. Montreal is the national port of Canada. Physical conditions have made it such, and on the progressive development and capable administration of the port depends not a local but a Domintion-wiide interest. For progressive development it is desirable that the Harbor Board should be persona grata to the ministry at Ottawa, a fact of which no one is more conscious than the recently resigned commissioners after a period of exceptional progress, and good service.
I would not go as far as the Montreal Gazette did.
Neither would I.

But I still maintain that when the chairman of a harbour commission is not only a strong political par-tizan, but takes an active part in political warfare; when he is the publisher of a newspaper which attacks the Government every morning, and when he assails the Minister of Marine and Fisheries under whom he is supposed to act-that is a condition of things which nobody in the House and nobody in the country would tolerate. I would not have been true to myself; I would not have been true to the position I occupy, had I been willing to permit such a condition to continue.

I do not want to assail the present Harbour Commissioners of Quebec, but I think the right hon. leader of the Opposition might complain if he were in my position. The first appointment made by the new harbour board was that of Captain Ambroise Landry as harbour master of the port of Quebec. Captain Landry was the man who sought to be my opponent in Bonaventure county four years ago. He was actually in the running; his nomination papers had been prepared, but he was pulled off by the Quebec committee, and
Mr. Philippe Furois put in his place. I think the new harbour board of Quebec must be pretty liberal in their views when they appoint as harbour master a man who had been willing to be a Conservative candidate in the constituency.
He is not a commissioner.

No, but he acts under these gentlemen who have been appointed by the present minister.

Quebec Harbour
Probably he was appointed because they wanted the hon. member to have no opposition the next time.

Any questions asked
from this side of the House are not by way of objection to items to provide for the development of our national ports. We are simply looking for information-because every member of the House was not invited to go to Quebec on that trip the other day. I myself was not invited. This resolution was placed on the Order Paper on the 24th of March. It was called almost every day, but was not gone on with until some members of the House had been invited to go and inspect these improvements. I am glad they did go there, because seeing is believing, and that applies to harbour works as well as to anything else. If you want to understand a harbour development, you have to see it. I do not blame the minister, as one of the representatives of the Quebec district, for his interest in Quebec harbour. He said that some were hungry who were not thirsty. I may say in answer that the minister is both hungry and thirsty to get this matter through in the form of a resolution rather than to take a chance with an item in the main estimates. The resolution is dated March 24, but it was not gone on with until the Progressives were invited to Quebec last Saturday. As I was not one of those invited, I may say to the minister that I do not know what it is to be either hungry or thirsty.
Order.

It does seem to me, Mr. Chairman, that there has been altogether too much politics in connection with the Quebec harbour since Confederation. I have a table here which was prepared the other day in answer to a question, giving certain figures and total expenditures with respect to the various ports in Canada. As I say, there has been too much politics and too little business in connection with the development of our national harbours, and the mixing up of politics with the matter, and the absence of business methods, has cost the country millions of dollars. It is true that terminal facilities are necessary at ports like Quebec and Montreal to take care of the increased business, but how is it that some of these ports are dealt with by resolution, while the others are left to shift for themselves in the main estimates?

Here is the port of Victoria, B.C., badly in need of a dry dock and terminals; what is going to be done there? What about Halifax, St. John, Toronto, Hamilton and other places which need adequate terminal facilities also and cannot get them? What I urge is that there be equality of treatment. I do not blame the minister for what has happened in the past; he has been in office only a few months. But I do not see any reason why there should be a change of officials and commissioners at the port of Quebec or the port of Montreal. If you want good government of a port and value for your money you must have continuity of officials, engineers, management, commissioners, and financing. Things must 'be done in a businesslike way. As it is now, the officials change with the Government, instead of the ports being administered by a permanent commission along business lines. A permanent commission would1 be in a far better position to decide as to how much dredging was to be done this year, how many immigration sheds and elevators, etc., should be provided, what would likely be the revenue from the port, and what increased business they could get.
Were not the harbour commissioners of Montreal and Quebec changed after 1911? Every Liberal that cropped up then was discharged.

I am not interested in the past or in politics in the way the hon. member is. He has politics for his breakfast, dinner and tea. I am not interested at all in that phase of the problem. Never mind what has happened in the past. Let us concern ourselves with the future. Let us get value for this money that the minister proposes to spend.
What does the minister mean by equipment of the port? I see by this statement and comparison of expenditures in harbours that only very small amounts were spent on Quebec harbour in the years when immigration was the greatest. In 1895-96 only $8,000 was spent, and there was a large immigration in that year. The next two years $6,000 was spent. In 1910-11 the amount was much greater, $392,000; in 1911-12, $529,000, and in 1914 $497,000. Of the entire expenditure of $11,000,000 on the Quebec harbour, $5,500,000 was spent between 1914 and 1918 while the war was on. During the war the port was able to take care of all the business, of all immigration navigation, including inward and outward bound traffic at no very great expense.

Quebec Harbour
I should like to see equality of treatment as between harbours and ports of this country. If the minister is prepared to go and do likewise for other ports and harbours that are badly in need of equipment and facilities, all very well and good. There are many places that want terminal facilities, but they have to pay for them. It does not do them very much good if they are hungry and thirsty in a terminal facilities sense, as they must provide for their terminal facilities themselves. It is the same with expenditures for post office facilities. I have no objection to the minister equipping Quebec harbour to make it fit for the business that will be done to-morrow, not only in an immigration sense, but a transportation sense, so that he will be able to take care of the great increase in navigation and general trade which will develop at the port in the near future. If the Government would extend the same treatment to other ports in the country and give them equality of treatment, I think such action would1 commend itself to the wisdom and judgment of the country generally.

May I say again to
my hon. friend from Toronto that the only reason why this is being done by way of legislation is because it is the law. It would be much easier to have an appropriation in the Estimates, as is done for Toronto, than to bring down legislation which is closely scrutinized by the House. But the law requires this procedure, and that is the only reason why we are proceeding in this way.
Most of the discussion that has taken place has arisen through a misapprehension.
I was very glad indeed to hear many hon. gentlemen speak of the magnificent-harbour of Quebec and say that it possessed all the facilities that are required. For this to be said in the House of Commons of Canada is a good advertisement of the port, and I am glad for that reason. I must once again try to impress upon the members of the committee that these advances are not for the purpose of adding to the facilities which now exist at the port. They are not, as my hon. friend who spoke on the other side some time ago suggested, for the purpose of improving the harbour, but they are for the purpose of maintaining the present facilities. This money is required to keep in good order the present equipment. Perhaps I had better read some of the items on which it is proposed to expend the money which is the subject of the present resolution.
The first item is to cover the cost of operating the commissioners' bucket ladder dredge, for three seasons. The dredging to be done during the above period, will consist of widening out the entrance of the river St. Charles Basin, widening out the basin to uniform lines and grades, and removing materials that accumulate at the various berths, so as to maintain the standard depth of 35 feet at low tide.
An item of $25,000 is required to cover the cost of alterations and mechanical improvements for Grain Elevator No. 2, in order to render the operations more efficient. Last year when the grain was sent to Quebec it all came at the same time, and the men had to work day and night. It was realized that some alterations were necessary to facilitate the work and make the operations more efficient.
Then there is an item of $18,000 for a new floor at shed No. 26, as the present old floor from long use has become so worn as to render the work of trucking goods a difficult and costly operation.
An item of. $20,598 is required to cover the cost of laying down a 21 inch tongued and grooved flooring in shed 19, and surfacing the quay front and open wharf at east end of shed with concrete. This work is required as the present shed and wharf planking is worn out and requires to be renewed.
For breakwater facing $53,470 is required. This is to cover the cost of rebuilding the river face of the old breakwater, for a length of 880 feet. This work is rendered necessary owing to the fact that the wharf, timbers from low water mark up to coping level have become decayed, and are no longer capable of retaining the filling materials in wharf.
Then $20,000 is required to cover the cost of certain alterations and additions to the foundations of shed 29 rendered necessary by the uneven settlement, due to the varying depths of the sand filling on which the shed has been erected.
An item of $30,000 is required to continue the work of reinstalling the long wharf at Indian Cove damaged by floods, and which work has already been approved to the extent of $53,900.
Six new floating fenders, amounting to $4,800, are required for the protection of vessels moored at pier No. 1.
Does my hon. friend want all the items?

It would be just as well.

Quebec Harbour

An item of $6,000 is required for painting the exposed iron works out of the dock front grain galleries which have not been painted since erection, and are now depreciating for want of painting.
An item of $5,000 is required to cover the cost of installing the machinery, electrical wiring, etc., in the travelling grain loader, structural steel work, which was completed last year and is now ready to receive machinery.
An item of $2,520 is required to cover the cost of laying down concrete paving, to replace the present decayed planking over the space between the landing sheds 18 and 26 along the dock front.
An item of $15,000 is required to cover the cost of laying down additional railway lines to serve the space at the western end of the embankment.
An item of $113,191 is required to cover the cost of constructing a fixed fender for a length of 300 feet along the river face of pier No. 1 at shed No. 26 berth. This fender will take the place of the present floating fenders at this part of the frontage and will keep vessels at this berth clear of the wharf, as do the present floating fenders, except in case of severe storms of easterly wind, when they may become misplaced or be carried away, thus allowing the vessel to come in contact with the wharf and be liable to injury. It is to avoid this contingency and to make this berth as secure as possible under all conditions, that it is considered advisable to replace the floating fenders by a fixed one for a length sufficient for one vessel's berth. Then:
Oil tank, $42,275.	_
The commissioners have entered into an agreement with a company for the erection of oiil tank for the supply of fuel oil to vessels henth in Louise docks. This amount is to cover the cost of laying down the pipes, installing the valves and other appliances required to complete the installation.
The commissioners have already entered into a contract with that company, and the amount which they will get from that company will be more than sufficient to pay the interest and the expenditure on that account.
Coal tower foundation, $17,572.
This is to cover the cost of replacing foundations for coal towers on the area leased of the Canadian Import Co. on the St. Charles frontage, and there is a continuation of a contract by which the commissioners lay down similar foundations in the wet dock for the same purpose.
Pliers at entrance of St. Charles river, $125,000.

This item is to cover the cost of constructing guide piers at the entrance to the river St. Charles quay frontage in order to protect vessels from the bank on the northern side of the entrance works and to render the navigation into this part of the docks easy and secure.
Landing stage and overhead passage at sheds Nos. 25 and 26, $30,000.
I think my hon. friend will see that this expenditure is not to provide new facilities in the harbour, but to keep the harbour in good order and maintain works that are already in existence.

I have a question to
ask. I happen to be one of those fortunate people who received the hospitality of the city and Harbour Commissioners of Quebec. My only disappointment is that before this question of harbour improvements came up we in Vancouver did not have our friends from the East visit us because then there would have been two resolutions introduced instead of one. Now my question is this:	I understand that considerable negotiations have taken place and many representations have been placed before the Government in respect to the harbour of Vancouver. I happen to be one of the members for that constituency and I can say there is a real need for dock accommodation, a great business need, which exists at the present time because the larger boats are compelled to go to Seattle to secure that accommodation. Is the Government willing to complete the dry dock which has been undertaken at Vancouver?

My hon. friend will
understand that I have no authority to speak on that subject. Perhaps the Minister of Public Works would know more about it than I do. All that I can tell my hon. friend is that works are going on in Vancouver harbour at the present time.
I refer to the dry dock.

I refer to the works
under the control of the Harbour Commission and undertaken on an advance made by this Parliament which has not yet been all expended. There still remains over two millions of that advance to be expended on the harbour of Vancouver and may I say this: Although some hon. member stated that Vancouver was paying interest on the advances made, the Government has not yet had the good fortune to receive any of that interest. I am sure, however, that Vancouver will pay its own way in the very near future on account of the very great facilities provided there.

Quebec Harbour
My question related particularly to the dry dock.

In regard to the dry
dock I am not in a position to make any promise.
For the minister's information I may say that I asked the same question of the Minister of Public Works and he had some reason which evaded the answer.
I see.
I shall therefore await the next opportunity of trying to get an answer to my question.
I will endeavour to secure the information for my hon. friend.
What work is to be done in Vancouver during the coming year with the $2,000,000 to which the minister has referred?
It will be necessary to complete the Ballantyne pier.
Is it not the custom to consult the Harbour Commissioners for the port during the season each year regarding the work projected?

The work is entirely under the control of the Harbour Commissioners. Of course, they submit for approval by the Governor in Council the various schemes upon which they decide, but we are not directing this work-they are doing it themselves.
Have they not submitted any proposals to the Governor in Council this year?
Not for the works of the present year.
In other words, there are no proposals at present before the Government that have not yet been dealt with?

No proposals for new work but, as I say, there is a balance of $2,000,000 to be expended there. Every advance must be approved by the Governor in Council, and any work to be done with that money must be approved by our engineers as well as by the Government.
Have any new proposals been submitted to the minister or to the Government, with regard to the projected work on the terminal railway and connection with North Vancouver?

Some proposals to that effect were submitted years ago but none have been submitted this year.
Mr. CLA.RK: Have those proposals been dealt with by the Government?
No.
Are they before the Government now?
They may still be in the department but they have not come under my consideration. I will be pleased to look into the matter if the hon. member desires it.
What amount of this $1,500,000 does the minister think will be necessary this year-I mean for maintenance, not for new construction?

As I have already
said, this money will not all be spent this year.

How much of it will be
expended this year?

I think perhaps one-third. This legislation is to enable the Government to make advances from time to time to the Harbour Commissioners for work which they desire to have done. Such work will have to be approved by the Government but it may not be carried out for two, three, four or five years.
Then why authorize such a large expenditure if it is not to be paid out this year?
My hon. friend will understand that if we have to come every year and ask for legislation of this kind it will take up a great deal of the time of Parliament.

I wonder if the minister is really still of the opinion that this vote should be asked for? I would like to point out to him in the first instance that he is putting in some new work-not very much but still some. I would also like to point out to him that works of a commercial character have never been paid for by harbour commissions. Take for example the coal plant. The coal plant at Montreal, I am informed, was installed by the commissioners at their own cost, they making some money out of it. It is the same with the oil plant. There does not seem to me any reason why the Quebec Harbour Commission should have to make these capital investments. However, I would like to
Quebec Harbour

seriously ask my hon. friend: Does he think at good business for this Government to issue bonds for any such purpose as mentioned? The explanation given by my hon. friend simply adds so much more force to what has been stated before as to the position of the Quebec Harbour Commission. They are owing the country these millions of dollars interest in arrears. Of course it is an investment, as my hon. friend knows, because the money could only be advanced in that way. It is intended to be, and really is an investment. In fact, it is an investment in Montreal, and will be an investment in Vancouver. But over and above all those tremendous losses, we find now that the business of this port obtained by the board is so small that they cannot keep up their current) painting. Surely, it is about time they stopped issuing bonds for any such purpose.

Is the fair wage
clause inserted in all contracts given by this corporation?
I have already said that I shall see that the Harbour Commission inserts such a clause. I am in favour of such a clause in all contracts on subsidized work.

When
was the last appropriation made for this port?

In 1917, five years
ago.
I think the hon. gentlemen is wrong about that. That was the date of the legislation. The hon. gentleman was not asking as to enabling legislation, but as to when the last appropriation was made.
The money has been paid from time to time since 1917. There is no more money now that can be advanced under the legislation.
Did I understand the hon. minister to say there had been no appropriation made for the harbour from 1919 to 1921?
No, I did not say that. I said the last legislation granting advances to the harbour was passed in 1917.
No appropriations have been made since then.

All these appropriations are part of the legislation.
Resolution reported, read the second time and concurred in. Mr. Lapointe thereupon moved for leave to introduce Bill No. 78, to provide for further advances to the Quebec Harbour Commissioners.
Motion agreed to and bill read the first time.
At six o'clock the House took recess.
After Recess
The House resumed at eight o'clock.

On motion of Hon. Ernest Lapointe (Minister of Marine and Fisheries) the House went into committee to consider the following proposed resolution, Mr. Gordon in the Chair:
That it is expedient to amend Section 477 of the Canada Shipping Act, chapter 113 of the Revised Statutes, 1906, by addling the provisions that ships of war and hospital ships belonging to such foreign nation or nations as may be specified by the Governor in Council; and ships registered in Canada engaged exclusively in fishing; shall be exempt from the payment of pilotage dues.

Under the Canada
Shipping Act all vessels entering certain ports have to pay pilotage dues whether they employ a pilot or not. Certain exceptions are made in all other countries, of course, there are a few exceptions under our own act. We want to add the exceptions mentioned in the resolution. The first is with respect to war and hospital ships- of friendly countries, of course; that is why the matter is to be dealt with by the Governor in Council. As to fishing vessels registered in Canada, the custom has been to exempt them from pilotage dues, but the law does not permit that. This legislation is simply to enable the matter to be dealt with as it has been, but in a legal way.

As I understand it, the act provides for the payment of pilotage dues by all vessels, with certain exceptions the minister has not mentioned. What are pilotage dues for? I must confess to a dismal ignorance of the subject. To whom are they payable?

The law makes it
obligatory on all vessels to pay pilotage dues. They are not compelled to take a pilot if they think they can enter the port without one, but they have to pay the dues, just the same.
Do they pay them to the Marine Department?
No, to the pilots themselves. They are usually formed into a corporation.
That is, the ships are corporations of course.

No. I mean the pilots. In Quebec, for instance, they have a corporation of pilots; the same is true of Montreal. The dues are fixed by the Governor in Council. The money goes into a general pilotage fund.
If they employ no pilot, whom do they pay?
The money goes into the common fund of the pilots.
That is, they pay the corporation?
Yes.

We are at peace with all countries' now; why does the Government ask to have reserved to itself the power to select and make favourites of nations? Is not the minister afraid that might possibly lead to Order in Council government?

I hope it will never
happen; on the other hand, there is no injury to anybody to leave the matter in the hands of the Governor in Council.

In the interests of the pilots themselves it is not wise that all these restrictions should be taken away. These men devote their whole lives to the business of piloting vessels into port, and they obtain their livelihood through the collection of dues from vessels that come in. Foreign vessels should
Montreal Harbour

be required to pay, because the pilots have no other means of earning a living and their work must all be done in the summer when the harbours are navigable, The exemption, therefore, should not go too far.

But should Parliament not say how far it should go? As I understand the way it reads, the Governor in Council could exempt the ships of half a dozen nations and subject the vessels of all the others to the payment of the dues. Why does the Governor in Council want the power of choosing between nations? Why should it be a respecter of nations when we are on the same terms with all?

Certainly we are on the same terms with all nations, but in the event of some nations not granting a similar privilege to British vessels, it is only fair that we should not grant these privileges to theirs.
That sounds reasonable. The purpose, then, is to grant them wherever corresponding privileges are granted to British vessels?

Yes.
Resolution reported, read the second time and concurred in. Mr. Lapointe thereupon moved for leave to introduce Bill No. 79, to amend the Canada Shipping Act (Pilotage).
Motion agreed to and bill read the first time.

On the motion of Hon. E. LAPOINTE (Minister of Marine and Fisheries), the House went into committee to consider the following proposed resolution, Mr. Gordon in the chair:
Resolved, (1) That it is expedient to provide that the Governor in Council may, from time to time, advance and pay to the Harbour Com-misstioners of Montreal, hereinafter called "the Corporation," in addition to the moneys, if any, heretofore authorized to be advanced to the corporation by the Governor in Council by any act, and which have not at the date of the passing of any act founded upon these resolutions, been so advanced, such sums of money, not exceeding in the whole the sum of five million dollars, as are required to enable the corporation to carry on the construction of terminal facilities in the harbour of Montreal, for which plans, specifications and estimates have been approved by the Governor in Council before the passing of the act founded upon these resolutions, and to construct such additional terminal facilities as are necessary to properly equip the said port.
(2)	That no such advance shall be made in respect of the construction of terminal facilities,

unless such detailed plans, specifications and estimates, for the works to be performed by the corporation and on which the money so to be advanced is to be expended, as are satisfactory to the Minister of Marine and Fisheries, have been submitted to and approved by the Governor in Council before any work on the same has been commenced.
(3)	That the corporation shall submit to the Minister of Marine and Fisheries for approval, monthly applications for such advances. With statements showing total expenditure on different items, in detail, and upon approval, authority for the payment of the amount applied for may be granted by the Governor in Council.
(4)	That the corporation shall upon any advances being made, deposit with the Minister of Finance debentures of the corporation equal in par value to the advance so made, repayable within twenty-five years from the date of issue and bearing interest payable half yearly, at the rate of five per cent per annum.
(5)	That the principal and interest of any sums advanced under any act founded on these resolutions shall be payable out of the revenue of the Corporation mentioned in section 8, of chapter 10, of the Statutes of 1896 (First Session), and shall be a charge thereon as if the sums so advanced had been borrowed by the corporation under said chapter 10.

It will perhaps interest the committee to know what is the financial position of the harbour of Montreal. There has been expended by the Government for the harbour at Montreal, through the Public Works Department, $1,055,725.08, and by the Harbour Commission $33,121,777.45, or a little over $34,000,000 altogether. The revenues of the port last year amounted to $2,891,274.42, or nearly $3,000,000, and the expenditure, including the interest paid on advances made by the Government, amounted to $2,724,100.02. So as may be seen, the port of Montreal is a paying proposition. As my hon. friend from South Wellington (Mr. Guthrie) said this afternoon, it is a good investment to make these advances to the Harbour Commissioners of Montreal. The commission needs the further amount stated in the resolution for completion of their works, and I am informed that for every addition which is going to be made to the port facilities, arrangements or contracts have already been entered into assuring a fair revenue to the commission.

I agree with the minister that this is a proposition entirely different from the proposal this afternoon, when this committee was asked to grant $1,500,000 to the Harbour Commissioners of the city of Quebec. I agree that the Montreal Harbour Commissioners have performed a very useful work for the Dominion of Canada. They have managed their business as a business should

Supply-Marine and Fisheries
be managed, and have been able at all times, I belreve, to meet their obligations. It has been a great boon to the whole Dominion of Canada to have such a harbour as we have in the city of Montreal. I believe, of course, that Montreal has been specially favoured by Providence in as much as it is an ocean port about 170 miles farther inland than the port of Quebec, and has great physical advantages. I think Montreal will in all probability be able to maintain its supremacy as a shipping port unless it be that in the future the tonnage of our ocean-going ships so greatly increases that they will not be able to go up as far as Montreal by reason of the levels of the St. Lawrence. At the present time, undoubtedly, Montreal is the great summer port of Canada. It has been well managed in the past, and I assume it will be well managed in the future. The proposal here is in the nature of a loan which will be returned to this Government. We will accept the bonds of the Harbour Commissioners, and those bonds bear interest sufficient to pay the cost to this country of carrying the loan, but in the case of the Quebec Harbour Commission which we discussed this afternoon, the proposal was not in the nature of a loan at all, but a straight grant of money without the chance of obtaining any interest or even the principal for many, many years to come. Personally, I would approve this resolution without further discussion.

The figures given by the minister disclose an investment that the country has in the port of Montreal of about $34,000,000. That is the aggregate of the various years right up from Confederation until now. The minister's figures also disclose a revenue last year that, if I figured it correctly in my mind as he read, amounted to about nine per cent. The commission pays, as I understand it, five per cent on its bonds. I do not think the whole investment is covered by bonds. Consequently, there will be more than four per cent of a surplus, or a surplus somewhere in the neighbourhood of $1,500,000. That surplus, of course, is not paid to the Dominion Treasury. It is held by the Harbour Commissioners. Is that surplus applied under the supervision of the Government towards improvements, towards extensions, towards facilities? If so, is this $5,000,000 in addition to the application of accrued surpluses by the commissioners, and what is the extent of the accrued surpluses that have been invested and are being invested this year?
Improvements made that have been paid from revenue income amount to $2,266,777.45.
Improvements from surplus income last year?
Yes.
Last year?
No, the figure I gave covers a number of years.
The surplus received last year, according to the minister's figures was about $1,500,000.
I do not think so.
I understood the minister to read two million odd as the disbursements and $3,800,000 as the revenue.

No. The revenue
last year was $2,891,274.42, and the expenditure $2,724,100.02.
I did not catch the figures the first time.

Let me state that last year the total quantity of grain shipped through the port of Montreal amounted to
135.000.	000 bushels, and of that quantity
55.000.	000 bushels was United States grain shipped to Montreal.

That is, 135,000,000
bushels through the port of Montreal as against 5,000,000 through the port of Quebec?

Yes.

I want to reiterate
